item.title: SCP-3186:
item.content:encoded:
This is a great example of a scip being humorous without crossing the line into -J territory. The line I found funniest is also the most deadpan:

Note that this phenomenon is purely visual in nature, and no actual alteration of the stars is taking place.

I would hope not!

item.title: SCP-3185: Minor Edit Request
item.content:encoded:
Any mail associated with SCP-3185 is to be removed from and confiscated for study.

Removed from what? I can guess at what the missing word is, but the rules as I understand them don't allow readers to edit an author's piece to insert missing words. (You could also just delete "removed from and" to make the sentence work, but again, I think that's beyond the scope of allowed reader edits.)

item.title: SCP-3184:
item.content:encoded:
This was a solid scip concept. I think the writeup could be condensed and shortened; many of the details are thoughtful, but ultimately not very engaging. The Series I scips you reference in comments, the ones I remember most vividly, were very short. Strangely enough, your writeup for this SCP strikes me as far more realistic, in that it provides details that a containment specialist would want to review before engaging with the anomaly. My guess is that this realism weakened the piece; after all, most real-life containment procedures would be relatively boring documents.

The brief description of Foundation detective work was good worldbuilding. Unfortunately I think the dry, clinical tone restraint of the SCP format didn't serve that worldbuilding goal; it felt too detailed when I first read it, despite its brevity. After some reflection, I think the problem was actually a lack of space for narrative beats. I'd enjoy reading a tale that depicts the Foundation investigation with a little more vibrancy and drama.

item.title: SCP-2718:
item.content:encoded:
Silly O5s! All that panic and at no point did anyone think to check, with the Foundation's usual clinical thinking, whether that was *a property of the Galapagos islands specifically…*

I mean, it's not like they are heavily populated - if they thought it could be endemic to death period and never been discovered, it'd be even easier for it to be a localised phenominon created by some nasty hiterto anomaly located in the region; which, without anyone going "hang on…" is going uncontained.

Heck, the very response of the O5s could *itself* be due to some sort of memetic effect…

item.title: SCP-3181:
item.content:encoded: The line about the trash cans not containing any bones was perfectly placed and camouflaged. My headcanon is that the Foundation is focused on investigating the wrong thing here, and some other entity is pleased with the success of its obfuscation. Is this scip actually contained? We'll never know for sure, but I love how clear it is that something more than "weirdly localized definition of a word" could be going on here. The dadaist-meme funniness of the word "boneless" takes the edge off of what could have been just as thoroughly creepy as the scip that used to be a library, but that's okay; the world don't need two antimemetic scips with that precise line of emphasis.

item.title: SCP-3180:
item.content:encoded:
I don't think this is a "Safe" SCP by current standards. Arguably it's Keter, because, as the author says above,

Rabbits can migrate, you miss one or two and they breed like, well, rabbits, so in a few years you've got the same problem again; dealing with this requires a large scale effort (you've got to comb every inch of half of Georgia), and the Foundation finds it easier to amnesticize ~20 people per year affected by this.

If the Foundation can't feasibly contain an anomaly, and constant vigilance and regular follow-up action is required in order to address instances' effects after-the-fact, that's Keter, right? I'm still learning, so I'm open to hearing explanations to the contrary.

item.title: SCCP-2930:
item.content:encoded: Well-written, but when specific background is necessary to understand why the reader should care about an article, and then the background is elided, it's an exercise in futility. Downvote.

item.title: SCP-3173:
item.content:encoded:
This is an extremely rough article with wince-inducing dialogue, but I agree with QuixoticQuasar that the scip concept has promise.

I was ready to downvote even before the vengeful doctor appeared, but that sealed it. That was one of the five worst "twists" in all of Series I-IV. Just deleting that entire section would vastly improve this article.

item.title: SCP-3170:
item.content:encoded:
I was hoping to see some negative/neutral discussion of this scip, because I can't see why its rating would be so low. I guess there's just not enough here for some folks? The only issue I found in the article was here:

Exhuming her body showed that its stomach had been stuffed with approximately 150 meters of Super 8mm footage of SCP-3170; portions of the film had been replaced with corneal tissue matching that of SCP-3170.

It wasn't entirely clear to me why they'd exhume and inspect her body. Other than that, I think this is well-written, and probably just needed more content to hook people in and get us to care more about the anomalous actress.
